newsitem.title: USA: Republicans see budget compromises, more work ahead.
newsitem.headline: Republicans see budget compromises, more work ahead.

text.p: Congressional Republicans struggled Friday to close ranks on a balanced budget plan, compromising on medical savings accounts, welfare and other issues but deferring politically tough decisions on Medicare.
"It was a very good day ... issue-wise we're about 85 percent through," Senate Budget Comittee Chairman Pete Domenici said after House and Senate Republican leaders emerged from day-long meetings.
Republicans agreed to a pilot programme allowing 500,000 seniors to set up medical savings accounts as an alternative to the regular Medicare programme.

But Domenici said lawmakers had not come together on two politically ticklish items -- whether to support Senate-passed plans forcing the affluent to pay higher Medicare premiums and gradually raise the program's eligibility age to 67 from 65.
Sources said House Republicans dug in their heels in on both issues, opposing the Senate.
"It's virtually impossible for the income-related premium," said one source. "The House is adamant."

Clinton has said he opposes raising the eligibility age, but might back a premium income test. The Senate plan would increase premiums for single seniors making more than $50,000 a year and couples with incomes over $75,000.

Republicans are trying to come to consensus on $115 billion in five-year Medicare reductions, about $15 billion in Medicaid savings and other spending cuts needed to implement a balanced budget deal with the White House.

Republicans plan to resume negotiations next week. Any agreements are only a first step. After they work out a coordinated bargaining position, Republicans must negotiate final legislation with President Clinton and Democrats.
Congressional leaders want to pass a final budget bill, and a companion measure cutting taxes by $85 billion by Aug 1.
The medical savings account agreement would let 500,000 seniors set up tax-free MSAs as an alternative to the regular Medicare programme. The Senate proposed only 100,000 accounts.
The White House and many Democrats oppose MSAs, saying they will attract wealthier, healthier recipients leaving sicker seniors in the Medicare programme and increasing costs.

The accounts are used in conjunction with high deductible insurance plans that kick in for medical emergencies. Seniors would be able to withdraw money for routine medical bills. Any funds remaining at the end of the year could be rolled over.
Republicans also agreed to a House plan letting states count Food Stamps and cash aid as wages for welfare recipients engaged in workfare programmes.

The House originally wanted to let states count a much wider array of federal assistance as compensation to sidestep a White House decision applying minimum wage laws to welfare programmes. The Senate had no provisions. The scope of workplace protections will still be at issue with the White House.
Domenici said lawmakers worked out housing and energy spending cuts and proposals to auction off part of the broadcast spectrum, but did not give details.
Aides also said the lawmakers were considering a proposal that would give states wide latitude to create their own children's health programmes.

The budget deal set aside $16 billion to provide health care for many of the nation's 10 million uninsured children. The House passed a plan giving states broad grants to design their own programmes, including health services.
The Senate plan required states to use the money for insurance and specified benefits including mental health aid.
State governors oppose the Senate plan, asking for the broadest possible latitude to design their own programmes.
A proposal under discussion would allow states to choose from a menu of insurance plans, possibly providing less coverage than the Senate.
